enrichment.short_title: Daniel v Drew: actual undue influence over elderly aunt's trust resignation
key_facts: Mrs Irene Margaret Drew, an 85-year-old aunt, resigned as trustee of Hyde Farm after pressure from her nephew Nicholas Daniel over farm repairs and trustee meetings.

Judge Weeks Q.C. set aside a memorandum and deed of retirement dated February 2002, finding Nicholas exploited her vulnerability and misrepresented that Stephen could not be appointed as her successor.
Nicholas visited alone, used a neighbour as witness, and avoided involving Mrs Drew's solicitors or her son Stephen.
Mrs Drew wanted to retire only if Stephen or his representative replaced her; the nephews opposed that condition.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from a deputy Chancery judge's decision setting aside trust retirement documents procured by alleged actual undue influence.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; the judge was entitled to find actual undue influence through improper pressure and misrepresentation, and the claim was not sterile.
enrichment.ratio: Actual undue influence is not confined to overt unlawful threats; vulnerability, forceful conduct and court references may be relevant, and Lord Eldon's inquiry into how intention was produced applies to both actual and presumed undue influence.
legal_issues: Whether Mrs Drew had to prove overt acts of improper pressure or coercion
Whether the judge wrongly elided actual and presumed undue influence by reference to vulnerability
Whether threatening court proceedings could amount to improper pressure in the circumstances
Whether relief was sterile because Mrs Drew wished to retire with a successor appointed

notes: Detailed VAT tribunal appeal on virtual assignment sale-and-leaseback; outcome and ECJ-derived principles are explicit.

enrichment.short_title: Abbey National v HMRC: VAT on virtual assignment sale-and-leaseback
key_facts: Abbey National sold about 1,000 properties to Mapeley and leased back premises it wished to occupy, using virtual assignments where landlord consent for leasehold transfers was unavailable.
The VAT tribunal held Mapeley's supply to Abbey was standard-rated agency and property management, not exempt letting, but that sub-tenant rents accrued to Mapeley under Schedule 10.
Virtual assignments passed economic benefits and burdens of shorter leases to Mapeley while Abbey remained legal lessee pending formal assignment.
Abbey paid a Principal Fee for occupation under the virtual leaseback arrangements.
enrichment.procedural_posture: High Court appeal and cross-appeal from a VAT and Duties Tribunal decision on the VAT treatment of a sale-and-leaseback using virtual assignments.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed and cross-appeal dismissed; the Principal Fee was consideration for an exempt letting by Mapeley, but paragraph 8(1) of Schedule 10 treated Mapeley as making the grant to undertenants.
enrichment.ratio: For Sixth Directive purposes a virtual assignment reproducing the essential features of a letting may be equated with a legal assignment; between Abbey and Mapeley the Principal Fee was paid for occupation pursuant to an agreement amounting to a letting despite Abbey's underlying leasehold title.
legal_issues: Whether Mapeley's supply to Abbey was exempt leasing or standard-rated services
Whether a virtual leaseback could confer a letting by Mapeley when it never held occupation rights
Construction of paragraph 8(1) Schedule 10 where sub-lease benefits were held in trust for Mapeley
Whether a reference to the ECJ was required

enrichment.short_title: Golobiewska v HMRC: inadequate reasons on car forfeiture restoration
key_facts: Mrs Golobiewska's Mercedes was seized at Dover in January 2000 when her friend Terlecki used it to smuggle cigarettes; the car was forfeited under section 139.
HMRC refused restoration under section 152; after review the VAT and Duties Tribunal found she knew Terlecki borrowed the car for smuggling.
The Tribunal held a four-day hearing but gave fragmented reasons for rejecting her denial of knowledge.
Laddie J dismissed her section 11 appeal; permission to appeal was limited to burden, standard of proof and adequacy of reasons.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Court of Appeal appeal on whether the Tribunal erred on burden and standard of proof and failed to give adequate reasons for its knowledge finding.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed on inadequate reasons alone; matter remitted to a differently constituted Tribunal; burden held to lie on the appellant under section 16(6).
enrichment.ratio: Section 16(6)(a) shifts burden to the Commissioners only where liability to a section 8 penalty is directly in issue; where a Tribunal effectively finds deliberate facilitation of smuggling it must explain why it rejected the owner's evidence.
legal_issues: Whether section 16(6)(a) placed the burden on HMRC because knowledge of smuggling amounted to section 8 conduct
Whether the criminal standard of proof applied to restoration appeals
Whether the Tribunal gave adequate reasons under English v Emery Reimbold
The scope of the Tribunal's fact-finding role under Gora

enrichment.short_title: Keenan: magistrates quashed over stop notice breach reasons
key_facts: Patrick Keenan built a hardcore track without planning permission at Well Close, Leigh; Woking Borough Council served enforcement and stop notices in September 2003.
Keenan said work finished on 20 September before the stop notice took effect; on 23 September he claimed to be servicing a motorcycle at Epsom College.
Neighbours Mr and Mrs Boroman said Keenan was on site with a JCB; planning officer Travis said he saw levelling work though he photographed only static vehicles.
Magistrates preferred Keenan's Epsom evidence corroborated by Mr Marsh and dismissed the prosecution.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal by way of case stated from magistrates' acquittal on a section 187(1) failure to comply with a stop notice.
enrichment.outcome: Decision quashed for inadequate reasons; matter remitted to a differently constituted bench; conclusion that no work occurred on 23 September was perverse unless Travis's evidence was rejected.
enrichment.ratio: Where the only witness to post-departure site activity described levelling in progress, magistrates could not rationally conclude no construction work occurred without expressly rejecting or explaining away that evidence; section 187(1B) causing or permitting also required consideration.
legal_issues: Whether magistrates were entitled to acquit on the criminal standard
Whether rejection of the Boromans' evidence left Travis as sole credible witness to work on site
Adequacy of reasons for preferring the defence account over Travis's levelling evidence
Whether section 187(1B) causing or permitting was adequately addressed

enrichment.short_title: Hinton v UEL: section 203 and whistleblowing compromise agreements
key_facts: Dr Hinton retired early from the University of East London under a compromise agreement dated 21 July 2003 settling employment and termination claims.
The agreement listed many claim types but omitted section 47B public interest disclosure detriment claims despite prior correspondence raising such allegations.
The employment tribunal held the agreement invalid under section 203 for omitting the particular proceedings; the EAT reversed, treating clause 9.1 as sufficiently broad.
Hinton issued tribunal proceedings on 23 October 2003 alleging continuing detriment from protected disclosures about financial irregularities.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from the Employment Appeal Tribunal on whether a compromise agreement precluded section 47B whistleblowing proceedings.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; contractually the agreement covered section 47B claims but failed section 203(3)(b) because it did not relate to the particular proceedings with sufficient particularity.
enrichment.ratio: Section 203 protects employees by requiring compromise agreements to identify particular proceedings clearly, by generic description or statutory reference; broad catch-all wording covering all statutory claims is insufficient even where the claim was previously raised.
legal_issues: Whether the agreement contractually compromised section 47B claims
Construction of 'relate to the particular proceedings' in section 203(3)(b)
Whether Lunt supports broad compromise wording without itemisation
Good practice for drafting valid compromise agreements

notes: Full TCC trial on Telecommunications Code objection; standing, expert evidence and dismissal are comprehensively reasoned.

enrichment.short_title: Petursson v Hutchison 3G: Code objection to 3G base station
key_facts: Claimants lived at 57 London Road Worcester near a Hutchison 3G base station installed on adjacent pub premises in August 2003.
They complained of headaches, nausea and disorientation attributed to emissions, but expert evidence showed exposures far below ICNIRP guidelines.
Early log entries recorded symptoms before the mast was operational; the claimants sold the property before trial.
Damages claims were abandoned; only removal or repositioning of apparatus was sought under paragraph 17 of the Electronic Communications Code.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Technology and Construction Court trial of a paragraph 17 Code objection to a 3G telecommunications base station.
enrichment.outcome: Claim dismissed for lack of standing after disposal of the property and on merits because material prejudice was not objectively established.
enrichment.ratio: Paragraph 17(6) requires objective proof that apparatus materially prejudices enjoyment of land; subjective fear or psychosomatic symptoms without causal evidence are insufficient, and owners who sell lose standing to seek removal orders.
legal_issues: Whether claimants retained standing after selling 57 London Road
Whether paragraph 17(6) prejudice is subjective or objective
Causation of alleged health effects from ICNIRP-compliant emissions
Reliability of claimants' contemporaneous log and symptom correlation evidence

enrichment.short_title: Orange PCS v Islington: conservation area and telecoms permitted development

statutes_considered.title: Town and Country Planning (General Permitted Development) Order 1995
Planning (Listed Buildings and Conservation Areas) Act 1990

key_facts: Orange PCS obtained prior approval under GPDO Part 24 for telecoms equipment at Canonbury Telephone Exchange but installation did not match approved plans.
Enforcement notices requiring removal were varied in January 2004 to require alterations bringing works into compliance.
Islington designated the Highbury New Park Conservation Area in October 2002, making the site Article 1(5) land excluding Part 24 antenna development.
In June 2004 the council withdrew the varied enforcement notices and issued fresh removal notices relying on loss of permitted development rights.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review challenge to withdrawal of varied enforcement notices after conservation area designation.
enrichment.outcome: Withdrawal notices quashed; Article 4 was the proper mechanism to restrict permitted development after designation rather than retrospectively denying crystallised prior approval rights.
enrichment.ratio: Once prior approval under Part 24 has crystallised the extent of permission, later conservation area designation does not automatically extinguish accrued rights to complete compliant development; Article 4 provides the lawful route to require fresh planning permission.
legal_issues: Whether conservation area designation revoked existing Part 24 prior approval rights
Construction of 'would consist of' in Schedule 2 Part 24 A.1(h)
Whether Article 4 directions are the correct remedy after designation
Whether judicial review was preferable to pursuing the enforcement appeal

enrichment.short_title: Watson v Dartford: prohibition after unlawful trial adjournment
key_facts: Watson faced magistrates' trial for careless driving, failing to provide a breath specimen and failing to stop after a December 2002 accident.
On 27 February 2004 justices refused a prosecution adjournment because witnesses Bulman and PC Hall were unavailable; on 1 March a new bench granted adjournment without changed circumstances.
Miss Bulman would have proved NFU insurance documents; PC Hall's evidence of transmission was unnecessary.
Business documents could have been admitted under section 27 of the 1988 Act or later under the 2003 Act without oral testimony.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application for prohibition before conclusion of magistrates' proceedings after an adjournment granted in breach of Acton Youth Court principles.
enrichment.outcome: Prohibition granted only to prevent oral evidence from Miss Bulman and PC Hall; justices to apply hearsay rules in force at the resumed trial date.
enrichment.ratio: Magistrates may not revisit and revoke an earlier refusal to adjourn absent a change of relevant circumstances; the prejudice from an wrongly granted adjournment is limited to excluding oral evidence that would not otherwise have been available.
legal_issues: Whether judicial review was premature before trial completion
Power of magistrates to revoke an earlier adjournment refusal
Extent of prohibition where business documents could be admitted without oral evidence
Whether trial should proceed under 1988 or 2003 hearsay provisions

enrichment.short_title: HST v SoS Transport: Immingham Outer Harbour HRO challenge
key_facts: ABP sought a Harbour Revision Order for five new roll-on roll-off berths at Immingham Outer Harbour, removing 22 hectares of intertidal mudflat bird habitat.
Competitor Humber Sea Terminal objected outside the statutory period and later applied for its own HRO for additional berths upstream.
The Secretary of State authorised the HRO in July 2004 relying on imperative reasons of overriding public interest and compensation agreements.
A proposed Phase 2 SPA extension covering the works area was not yet classified though treated under PPG9 precautionary policy.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Section 44 Harbours Act challenge to the Immingham Outer Harbour Harbour Revision Order 2004 on environmental and procedural grounds.
enrichment.outcome: Application dismissed on all grounds; Basses Corbieres did not apply without an allegation of Birds Directive breach, and the environmental statement and compensation agreement were lawful.
enrichment.ratio: Sites treated as SPAs under precautionary policy are not 'should have been classified' sites within Basses Corbieres unless non-classification itself breached Directive obligations; compensation measures under Regulation 53 need not be in the ES if not main or likely significant effects of the project.
legal_issues: Whether Basses Corbieres precluded IROOI for an unclassified potential SPA
Whether the environmental statement was invalid for omitting compensation realignment schemes
Whether the compensation agreement secured Natura 2000 coherence under Regulation 53
Failure to assess in-combination effects with HST's separate HRO proposal

enrichment.short_title: Circular Facilities v Sevenoaks: Part IIA remediation notice appeal
key_facts: Sevenoaks served a remediation notice on Circular Facilities as an appropriate person for methane and carbon dioxide from decomposing organic matter at Well Close, Leigh.
The site was infilled clay pits developed for housing in 1980; a 1978 soil report disclosed black organic matter and gas bubbling in trial pits.
CFL's controlling mind Mr Ketteringham denied knowing of organic material until 2002, relying on Mr Scott to supervise development.
The district judge inferred CFL must have known but did not clearly find personal knowledge or impute Mr Scott's agency knowledge.
enrichment.procedural_posture: First High Court appeal under Regulation 13 against a magistrates' court upholding a Part IIA remediation notice for knowingly permitting contamination.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; knowledge finding quashed for inadequate reasons; matter remitted for retrial though section 78F(9) does not require knowledge of resulting harm from substance A.
enrichment.ratio: A finding that a developer knowingly permitted organic material requires clear fact-finding on who knew what and why; availability of a soil report on the planning register is insufficient alone, and section 78F(9) extends liability to substances produced by biological or chemical processes affecting a known substance.
legal_issues: Whether CFL or Mr Ketteringham knew of buried organic matter between 1979 and 1985
Whether knowledge of the 1978 report sufficed for 'knowingly permitted'
Imputation of Mr Scott's knowledge as CFL's agent or partner
Whether knowingly permitted requires awareness of potential harm from chemical or biological processes
